documents.section_title: From zero to your first event, in about five minutes
documents.title: From zero to your first event, in about five minutes
documents.content:
1. Quickstart

 

## From zero to your first event, in about five minutes

 

Ravensight is hosted. You do not run a server, you point your game at ours.

 

1. **Create an account.** Sign in at `https://app.ravensight.io` through RealitySE, the identity system Ravensight runs on. Use email and password, or one of the SSO providers: Apple, Google, Facebook, GitHub, Twitch, Xbox, or Steam.
 
1. **Create a project.** A project is one title, and it holds one game per environment. The first time you sign in the dashboard asks for a name, an id and an engine, and creates the project with its production environment in one step. Every feature is available right away, no upgrade required. See [Projects and environments](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#projects) for the shape.
 
1. **Copy the ingest key.** Each environment has its own. It is shown once on the confirmation screen and looks like `gt_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx`. It is publishable: safe to ship inside your game binary, since it can only create sessions, read the tracking on/off switch and the AI suggestions feed, submit player reports and submit doctor reports. It cannot read analytics or manage your account. If you lose it, rotate it from **Settings > Projects** for a new one.
 
1. **Add the autoload.** Copy `Ravensight.gd` into your Godot project, e.g. `res://autoload/Ravensight.gd`. Open **Project > Project Settings > Autoload**, add the script, name it `Ravensight`, and enable it. In the Inspector, set `api_url` to your Ravensight base URL (no trailing slash, no `/api/v1`) and `ingest_key` to the key from step 3. Not on Godot? Install the SDK for your engine from the [SDK list](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#platform-support) instead (Unity, Unreal, web, iOS, Android, C++ or Odin), or call the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#http-api) directly from anything else.
 
1. **Send your first event.** Call `track_event()` from anywhere in your game.
 
1. **See the dashboard.** Pick your project in the switcher, and the environment beside it if the project has more than one. The SDK batches and sends events shortly after you call `track_event()`, so they typically show up within a few seconds, no restart needed.

 

Godot, res://autoload/ravensight.gd

 

```
Ravensight.track_event("level_completed", {
    "level": 3,
    "score": 15000,
    "time_seconds": 87.4
})
```

 

**Not on Godot?** The same account and ingest key work against the plain [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#http-api): three headers and a JSON body from any engine or client that can make a POST request.

2. Install an SDK

 

## Where the SDKs run

 

Every SDK ships as source and speaks plain HTTPS to the same four endpoints. There is no prebuilt binary and no platform specific code path in any of them, so an SDK works wherever its engine exports. The C++ and Odin SDKs link libcurl for the HTTP calls.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Support matrix
documents.content:
### Support matrix

 

| SDK | Desktop | iOS | Android | Web | Console |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Godot | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, on the web export | Yes, subject to cert |
| Unity | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, on WebGL | Yes, subject to cert |
| Unreal | Yes | Yes | Yes | No web target in UE5 | Yes, subject to cert |
| JavaScript (web and Node) | Yes, in Electron or Node | Yes, in a web view | Yes, in a web view | Yes | Not applicable |
| C++ | Yes, C++17 plus libcurl | Yes, links libcurl | Yes, links libcurl | Not applicable | Yes, subject to cert |
| Odin | Yes, via libcurl binding | Untested | Untested | Not applicable | Untested |
| iOS native Swift | Yes, macOS 12+ | Yes, iOS 15+ | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| Android native Kotlin | Not applicable | Not applicable | Yes, minSdk 24 | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| Any engine via HTTP | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, subject to cert |

 

These are honest cells, not a marketing grid. Because everything is an HTTPS request, an SDK runs on any target its engine can export to, and we have not special cased a single platform. What we have not done is ship a title on every one of them, so treat the mobile and console columns as "nothing in the way" rather than "verified in a submitted build".

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Consoles
documents.content:
### Consoles

 

Nothing in any SDK is blocked on a console. What is blocked is everything else about console networking: each platform holder requires that outbound traffic, privacy disclosure, and any data collection be declared and approved as part of certification, and NDA restrictions mean we cannot ship console specific code publicly anyway. Ravensight is an ordinary HTTPS call from your title's own network stack, and passing cert with it is the developer's responsibility, exactly as it would be for a leaderboard or a patch notes fetch.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Mobile privacy
documents.content:
### Mobile privacy

 

Ravensight does not touch an advertising identifier. Every SDK generates its own random device id on first run and stores it locally: 16 random bytes written as 32 lowercase hex characters, a hyphen, and the OS name, so `3f9ac2e17b5d4c0e8a61f2b9d7c04e5a-android` is what one looks like. No IDFA on iOS, no Android advertising id, no hardware identifier, and no IP based fingerprinting. That id is meaningless outside your game's own data, and nothing in Ravensight ever joins it to a name, an email or an account, because the SDK has no field for any of those.

 

An event row holds the game id, the device id, the session id, the event name, a timestamp, and the level, platform, version and payload you sent. It holds no IP address, user agent or location, and it is deleted after 90 days. Two things outlive that window: one record per game and device with the first day it was seen, kept for the game's lifetime so lifetime and new-player counts stay correct, and any feedback text a player typed, kept until you delete it or the game.

 

**No App Tracking Transparency prompt is required for Ravensight.** Apple defines tracking as linking data collected from your app about a user or device with data collected from other companies' apps, websites or offline properties for targeted advertising or advertising measurement, or sharing it with a data broker. Ravensight does neither: the id is yours alone, it is never combined with another company's data, and nothing reaches an ad network or a data broker. So on Ravensight's account you do not need to call `requestTrackingAuthorization`. If something else in your app does track across companies, that decision is unchanged by this.

 

Two SDK calls exist for studios that show their own consent screen. Ravensight ships no consent UI; wire these to your own settings menu if your audience or your lawyer wants one.

 

- `Ravensight.set_tracking_enabled(false)` stops the SDK sending anything: queued events are dropped, no further batch is flushed, and the choice is saved locally so it survives a restart until you call it with `true`.
 
- `Ravensight.reset_device_id()` deletes the saved id, generates a new random one and ends the current session, so a player can start a fresh analytics identity from your game's own settings. Rows already stored under the old id are not rewritten; they expire with the 90-day window, or sooner if you delete the game.

 

You do still have disclosure obligations, and they are yours rather than ours, because Apple and Google ask the publisher of record. The answers below cover what Ravensight collects on its own account; add whatever your own events carry on top, and if you send something personal, disclose it.

 

- **App Store privacy details.** Declare **Device ID** under Identifiers and **Product Interaction** under Usage Data, both under **Data Not Linked to You**, purpose **Analytics**, and answer **Data Not Used to Track You**. Add **Crash Data** under Diagnostics only if you send crash events; Ravensight has no crash reporter of its own.
 
- **Apple privacy manifest.** Add the two `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes` entries below to your `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, with `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked` false and `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking` false on both, and `NSPrivacyTracking` false. Ravensight adds no `NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes` entries of its own: it reads and writes one file in your game's own user directory and calls no required-reason API, so leave whatever your engine's export already declares exactly as it is.
 
- **Android.** The `android.permission.INTERNET` permission is the only one any SDK needs. No `AD_ID` permission, and nothing that triggers a runtime permission dialog. In the Play Console Data safety form declare **Device or other IDs** and **App interactions** as collected, not shared, for Analytics, not for advertising; answer yes to encrypted in transit, because every request is HTTPS; and answer yes to a deletion path, which is the reset call above plus deleting the game.

 

PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, the Ravensight entries

 

```
<key>NSPrivacyTracking</key>
<false/>
<key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes</key>
<array>
  <dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
    <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeDeviceID</string>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
    <array>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAnalytics</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
    <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeProductInteraction</string>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
    <array>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAnalytics</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
</array>
```

 

**What our sub-processors see**, so your "shared with third parties" answer is honest. The event stream is stored with our cloud, event database and operational database providers, who process it only to run Ravensight for you. When you use the AI analyst, the model provider receives the text a player typed into feedback and the rows and totals the analyst's tools queried, under contract; it never receives a player's report image. The embedding provider receives feedback text so you can search it. A product analytics service runs in the dashboard and on this website, never inside a game. Nothing reaches an ad network or a data broker, and nothing is sold. Both stores treat a service provider acting on your instructions as your own processing rather than sharing, which is why "not shared" is the correct answer. The [privacy policy](https://www.ravensight.io/privacy/) names every provider.

 

Ravensight itself is the processor here, not the controller. What ends up in an event payload is entirely what you chose to put there, so if you send something personal, disclose it.

 

#### What your privacy label can say

 

These are the answers for a game that uses Ravensight and nothing else that collects data. Each row says why, against the store's own definition, so you can defend it in review. Apple's rule for "not linked": direct identifiers are stripped before collection and you never try to link the data back to a person afterwards. Ravensight never collects a direct identifier in the first place, and there is no account to link to.

 

App Store privacy details

 

| Data type | Answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identifiers: Device ID | Collected. Analytics. Data Not Linked to You. Data Not Used to Track You. | A random per-install id that is never joined to a name, email or account, and never combined with another company's data, so it meets neither the "linked" test nor the tracking definition. |
| Usage Data: Product Interaction | Collected. Analytics. Data Not Linked to You. Data Not Used to Track You. | Event names, levels and session timing from your own game only, stored against the same unlinked id and used for nothing but your dashboard. |
| Diagnostics: Crash Data | Only if you send crash events. Same answers as above. | Ravensight has no crash reporter; a crash you report as an event is Product Interaction unless it carries a stack trace, in which case declare Crash Data too. |
| User Content: Other User Content | Only if you enable player feedback or Player Reports. Analytics. Not Linked. Not Used to Track. | Free text a player types and any image they attach are stored under the device id until you delete them; disclose what your players can type. |
| Contact Info, Location, Financial Info, Health, Browsing History, Search History, Purchases | Not collected. | The SDK has no field for any of these, and the privacy policy commits that it never will. |

 

Google Play Data safety

 

| Question or data type | Answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Device or other IDs | Collected. Not shared. Analytics. Not used for advertising or marketing. | The random per-install id above; it leaves your game only for Ravensight's own storage, which Play treats as your processing, not sharing. |
| App activity: App interactions | Collected. Not shared. Analytics. | Your gameplay events, under the same id, used only for your dashboard. |
| App info and performance: Crash logs | Only if you send crash events. | Ravensight has no crash reporter of its own. |
| Messages or other user-generated content | Only if you enable player feedback or Player Reports. | Text a player types is stored until you delete it and reaches the model provider for analysis under contract. |
| Is the data encrypted in transit? | Yes. | Every SDK talks to Ravensight over HTTPS only. |
| Is there a way to request deletion? | Yes. | `reset_device_id()` severs the player from their history and the old rows expire within 90 days; deleting the game removes everything at once. |
| Is collection required or optional? | Optional if you wire `set_tracking_enabled(false)` to a setting, otherwise required. | The switch is persisted and sends nothing while off; Ravensight ships no consent screen, so this one is your call. |

 

For a game that runs no ads, the one sentence this lets you put on your store page, and mean it: **"No ads, no tracking, no account needed."** If you later add an ad network, an attribution SDK or a sign-in, revisit every row above, because the first two are exactly what the tracking definition is about.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Ravensight.gd
documents.content:
3. Godot SDK reference

 

## Ravensight.gd

 

One autoload script. It owns device identification, session creation, batching, retries, and the offline queue, so your game code only ever needs to call `track_event()`.

 

Code samples scroll horizontally when needed. Focus a sample and use the arrow keys, or swipe to read a long line.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Exported properties
documents.content:
### Exported properties

 

Set these in the Inspector after adding the autoload.

 

| Property | Type | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_url` | String | `https://your-ravensight-instance.example.com` | No trailing slash, no `/api/v1`: the SDK appends the path itself. |
| `ingest_key` | String | `gt_live_your_ingest_key_here` | The publishable key from your game's confirmation screen. |
| `game_version` | String | `1.0.0` | Reported to the server as the client's game version. |
| `max_queue_size` | int | `100` | Max unsent events kept in memory. Oldest are dropped first once full. |
| `handle_quit` | bool | `true` | The SDK sets `auto_accept_quit` to false, flushes on a close request (and the Android back button when `quit_on_go_back` is on), then calls `get_tree().quit()` itself within 1.5 seconds. Set false if your game manages quitting; the SDK then only flushes. |

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Public functions
documents.content:
### Public functions

 

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `track_event(event_name: String, data: Dictionary = {})` | Queue an event. Safe to call before the session is ready: it is queued and sent once a session exists. |
| `flush()` | Force an immediate flush attempt. No-op if nothing is queued, no session is ready, or a flush is already in flight. |
| `submit_feedback(message: String, category: String = "", rating: int = 0)` | Send free-form player feedback. `category` and `rating` (1 to 5) are optional. Requires an active session; unlike `track_event()`, a call made before one exists fails immediately rather than queueing. |
| `set_tracking_enabled(enabled: bool)` | Player opt-out. `false` drops queued events, stops every flush and saves the choice locally so it holds across restarts; `true` turns sending back on, and does nothing for a player who never opted out. For studios that show their own consent screen; Ravensight ships no consent UI. |
| `reset_device_id()` | Deletes the saved device id, generates a new random one and ends the current session, so a player can start a fresh analytics identity from your settings menu. |
| `fetch_suggestions()` | Experimental. Requests AI-generated design suggestions for your game; result arrives on the `suggestions_received` signal. |

 

Call `Ravensight.is_tracking_enabled()` (or read `Ravensight.tracking_enabled`) at any time to check whether events are being collected. It is false when the server-side kill switch is off or the player has opted out.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Signals
documents.content:
### Signals

 

| Signal | Fires when |
| --- | --- |
| `session_ready` | A session token has been issued and is ready to use. |
| `session_failed(reason: String)` | Session creation fails outright. |
| `tracking_disabled(source: String)` | Tracking has stopped. `source` is `"server"` when the kill switch is off for this game, or `"player"` when the player opted out. Fires at boot, on `set_tracking_enabled(false)`, and mid-run if the server refuses a new session because the kill switch was turned off. |
| `events_flushed(count: int)` | The server answered a batch with success. `count` is the number of events sent in that batch, which can be more than the server stored: an event timestamped more than 90 days ago is dropped (see [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#http-api)). |
| `flush_failed(reason: String)` | A batch flush attempt fails. The SDK retries automatically; you do not need to. |
| `feedback_submitted` | A feedback submission is accepted. |
| `feedback_failed(reason: String)` | A feedback submission fails, including `"no_session"` when called too early. |
| `suggestions_received(suggestions: Array)` | Experimental. Carries the result of `fetch_suggestions()`. |
| `event_tracked(event_name: String, data: Dictionary)` | Every time `track_event()` queues an event, with the data actually queued (playtest tags included in a playtest run). Use it to mirror tracked events elsewhere in the running game. |

 

```
func _ready():
    Ravensight.session_ready.connect(func(): print("ready"))
    Ravensight.session_failed.connect(func(reason): print("session failed: ", reason))
    Ravensight.tracking_disabled.connect(func(source): print("tracking off: ", source))
    Ravensight.events_flushed.connect(func(count): print("sent ", count, " events"))
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Offline queue and backoff
documents.content:
### Offline queue and backoff

 

Every `track_event()` call adds to an in-memory queue. The SDK flushes it via `POST /api/v1/track/batch`, up to 50 events per request, looping until the queue is empty. If the server is unreachable, events stay queued (up to `max_queue_size`, oldest dropped first once full) and are retried with exponential backoff, starting at 10 seconds and doubling up to a 5 minute cap. If the server responds 429, the SDK backs off using the server's `Retry-After` value when one is given, and keeps the events queued for the next attempt: you do not need to handle this yourself.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Kill switch
documents.content:
### Kill switch

 

On boot, the SDK calls `GET /api/v1/settings` once with `ingest_key`. If tracking is off for your game, it goes idle for that run: no session is created and nothing is sent, and the `tracking_disabled` signal fires with source `"server"`. Flip `trackingEnabled` from the dashboard's game settings and it takes effect on the game's next launch, no update required.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Player Reports
documents.content:
### Player Reports

 

Add an optional in-game form that captures the current game screen, lets players highlight or hide an area, and sends a short message. Bind the reporting action to a key, controller input or pause-menu button. The dashboard groups reports into issues and tracks fixes through verification.

 

Download [Ravensight.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/Ravensight.gd), [RavensightReports.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/RavensightReports.gd) and [RavensightReportOverlay.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/RavensightReportOverlay.gd). Add the latter two as children of the Ravensight autoload, named RavensightReports and ReportOverlay. Bind `ravensight_report` in Input Map. The overlay captures only the game viewport and never pauses multiplayer.

 

Reports use your existing event allowance and prepaid balance automatically. A text report uses 1 event; a screenshot adds 20,000 usage events covering processing, storage and delivery. There is no separate screenshot budget to configure. Failed or canceled uploads release their reserved usage. Retention and file limits are listed in Settings. Text-only reporting remains available if capture or upload fails. Screenshots are not automatically sent to AI providers.

documents.content:
4. JavaScript SDK reference

 

## The ravensight package for browser games and Node

 

One zero-dependency client for browser games and Node 18 or newer, shipped as both ESM and CommonJS. It owns sessions, batching, the offline queue, rate limits and the server-side kill switch, so your game code calls `init()` once and `track()` from then on.

 

Code samples scroll horizontally when needed. Focus a sample and use the arrow keys, or swipe to read a long line.

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Install
documents.content:
### Install

 

```
npm install ravensight
```

 

There is no build step for consumers. It suits Phaser, PixiJS, three.js, Excalibur and hand written canvas games. Godot HTML5 exports use the [Godot SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#godot-sdk) instead.

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Quickstart

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Options
documents.content:
### Options

 

Pass these to `new Ravensight(options)`.

 

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ingestKey` | required | Your publishable `gt_live_...` key. Safe to ship in a client build. |
| `apiUrl` | `https://api.ravensight.io/api/v1` | `/api/v1` is appended if you leave it off. |
| `gameVersion` | `'1.0.0'` | Reported with the session. |
| `platform` | auto | `'web'` in a browser, `node-<platform>` in Node. |
| `autoFlushMs` | `15000` | Flush interval. `0` flushes only on demand. |
| `maxQueueSize` | `500` | Offline queue cap. The oldest events are dropped first. |
| `storage` | auto | Anything with `getItem` and `setItem`. Holds the device id. |
| `deviceId` | auto | Overrides the generated device id. |
| `enabled` | `true` | Pass `false` to start opted out. |
| `fetch` | global | Inject a custom fetch. |
| `debug` | `false` | Logs SDK activity to the console. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Methods
documents.content:
### Methods

 

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `await rs.init()` | Reads the kill switch from `GET /api/v1/settings`, then opens a session. Resolves with `{ trackingEnabled, sessionReady }` and never throws on a network failure. If tracking is off for your game, the queue is cleared and nothing further is sent. |
| `rs.track(event, data?)` | Queues an event and records its timestamp at the moment of the call. Safe before `init()`. Returns `false` when tracking is off. |
| `await rs.flush()` | Sends what is queued now and resolves with `{ sent, queued }`. Concurrent calls are safe. |
| `await rs.submitFeedback(message, category?, rating?)` | Sends player feedback. `category` is one of the values below, exported as `FEEDBACK_CATEGORIES`. `rating` is an integer from 1 to 5. Leave either out with `undefined`, `null` or an empty string. Anything else is invalid and throws before any request is made, with code `invalid_category` or `invalid_rating`; an empty message throws `empty_message`. |
| `rs.setEnabled(bool)` | Local opt in and opt out. `false` stops sending and clears anything queued. The SDK does not store the choice: keep it in your own settings and call this before the first event on every launch. |
| `await rs.setDeviceId(id)` | Changes the device id, for example after a player signs in on a shared machine. Queued events are flushed first under the old session, then the session is dropped and the new id is stored. The next flush opens a new session lazily. Setting the current id again does nothing. |
| `await rs.resetDeviceId()` | The same with a fresh random id, which it resolves with. Use it for a reset analytics id button. |
| `await rs.dispose({ flush = true, timeoutMs = 2000 })` | Shuts the client down and resolves with `{ sent, dropped }`. It flushes by default, bounded by `timeoutMs`, even if `init()` was never called. Events in a request that timed out count as dropped even if the request later lands. Pass `{ flush: false }` to discard the queue. After dispose, `track()` returns `false` and `setDeviceId()` and `resetDeviceId()` reject with code `disposed`. |
| `await rs.fetchSuggestions()` | Experimental. The AI-generated design suggestions for your game, empty until a weekly digest has run. The shape may change, so do not build game logic on it. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Feedback categories
documents.content:
### Feedback categories

 

| Category | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `bug` | Something is broken. |
| `suggestion` | An idea or a change the player wants. |
| `complaint` | Something the player dislikes. |
| `praise` | Something the player enjoyed. |
| `playtest` | Notes from a playtest session. |
| `other` | Anything else. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: How delivery works
documents.content:
### How delivery works

 

- **Batches of 50.** The server's limit per request. A flush keeps sending batches until the queue drains.
 
- **Offline queue of 500.** Events wait while the network is down, up to `maxQueueSize`. Past that the oldest are dropped, so the newest are kept. An event leaves the queue only once the server accepts it.
 
- **401** means the session expired: the SDK opens a new one and sends the same batch again.
 
- **429** honors `Retry-After`. Without that header the SDK backs off exponentially from 10 seconds up to 5 minutes. The queue is held, never discarded.
 
- **400** halves the batch and retries, down to a single event. An event still rejected on its own is dropped so it cannot block the rest.
 
- **Page hide.** When the page goes hidden the SDK sends one last batch, preferring `fetch` with `keepalive`. Where that is unavailable it falls back to `navigator.sendBeacon`, which cannot set headers, so the session token travels in the JSON body as `sessionToken`, never in the URL.
 
- **No duplicates.** The SDK never sends a batch again while it is still in flight, so a batch cut off by a real page unload can be lost rather than counted twice.

 

Session creation and tracked events are rate limited per game, not per client. See [Usage, billing and limits](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#limits).

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: What the dashboard reads
documents.content:
### What the dashboard reads

 

The dashboard gives meaning to some fields and event names. Name your events with these in mind.

 

- **One place per event.** `level`, `location` and `track` in the event data fold into one place, and the first non-empty one wins, in that order. The level funnel, per-level deaths and journeys only see events that have a place.
 
- **Event names.** A name containing `start`, `begin` or `enter` is a level start; `complet`, `finish`, `win` or `clear` is a completion; `died`, `destroyed` or `killed` is a death. These are lowercase substring matches.
 
- **`rs_kind` overrides the name.** Set `rs_kind` in the event data to `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death` or `none` and it is read before the name. `none` opts an event out, so `checkout_started` is not a level start. An unknown value falls through to the name match. Keys that start with `rs_` are reserved for Ravensight.
 
- **Potentially stuck** is one event repeated 10 or more times at the same level in a session of fewer than 20 events. The same event at a new level each time is movement, not stuck.

 

```
rs.track('boss_phase_begin', { level: 'castle', rs_kind: 'none' });
rs.track('run_over', { level: 'castle', rs_kind: 'death' });
```

 

The full rules, including the player flags, are in [how the built-in detections read your events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#detection-rules).

### Privacy

 

The SDK generates a random device id and stores it under `ravensight_device_id`. It collects no hardware identifier, advertising id or personal data, only the events you send. documents.title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.content:
5. HTTP API

 

## Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot

 

Building for the web or Node? The [JavaScript SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#javascript-sdk) wraps everything below in a zero-dependency client with batching, an offline queue, and tab-close flushing. Unity developers use the [Unity SDK](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unity). Everything else speaks plain HTTP.

 

The Godot SDK is a client for this same surface. If you're on Unity, Unreal, a browser game, or anything else, this is what to call directly. The ingest endpoints answer any web origin, so browser games on GitHub Pages, itch.io or your own site need no CORS setup.

 

Base URL

 

```
https://api.ravensight.io
```

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/session
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/session

 

Opens a session for a device. Auth: `X-API-Key` (your ingest key). The game identity comes from the key, never from the body.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/session
X-API-Key: gt_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "deviceId": "3f9ac2e17b5d4c0e8a61f2b9d7c04e5a-windows",
  "gameVersion": "1.4.2",
  "platform": "Windows"
}
```

 

Response, 201

 

```
{
  "token": "st_9f2c...redacted",
  "expiresAt": "2026-08-29T16:00:00.000Z",
  "expiresIn": 86400
}
```

 

Errors: `400 missing_device_id` when `deviceId` is absent, `401 invalid_api_key` or `missing_api_key`, `403 tracking_disabled` when the game's kill switch is off, `429 rate_limited` at more than 60 session creations per minute for the game.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: GET /api/v1/settings
documents.content:
### GET /api/v1/settings

 

Reads the tracking kill switch. Auth: `X-API-Key`.

 

Response, 200

 

```
{ "trackingEnabled": true }
```

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/track
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/track

 

Sends a single event. Auth: `X-Session-Token` (from step above).

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/track
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "event": "level_completed",
  "data": { "level": 3, "score": 15000, "time_seconds": 87.4 },
  "timestamp": <unix seconds, within the last 90 days>
}
```

 

Response, 202

 

```
{ "accepted": 1 }
```

 

`timestamp` is optional, in unix seconds, and defaults to the time the server receives the event. An event whose timestamp is more than 90 days old is dropped: it is not stored and not charged, and it is counted as `timestamp_too_old` on the Implementation health card. The request still succeeds, so `accepted` can be lower than the number of events you sent, on this endpoint and on `/track/batch`.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/track/batch
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/track/batch

 

Sends up to 50 events in one call. Same auth as `/track`.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/track/batch
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "events": [
    { "event": "level_started", "data": { "level": 3 } },
    { "event": "checkpoint_reached", "data": { "idx": 2 } }
  ]
}
```

 

Response, 202

 

```
{ "accepted": 2 }
```

 

Errors: `400 invalid_batch` when `events` is missing or empty, `400 batch_too_large` above 50 events, `400 missing_event` if any entry lacks an `event` name.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: GET /api/v1/agent/suggestions
documents.content:
### GET /api/v1/agent/suggestions

 

Experimental, machine-readable design suggestions from your weekly digest. Auth: `X-API-Key`. Returns an empty array until a digest has run for your game.

 

```
{ "suggestions": [] }
```

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/feedback
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/feedback

 

Auth: `X-Session-Token`.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/feedback
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "message": "Level 3's second checkpoint feels unfair.",
  "category": "suggestion",
  "rating": 4
}
```

 

Response, 201

 

```
{ "id": "66c1f2a9d4e8b0021f9a7c31" }
```

 

`category` and `rating` are both optional. When present, `category` must be one of `bug`, `suggestion`, `complaint`, `praise`, `playtest`, or `other`.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: Errors
documents.content:
### Errors

 

| Status | Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `missing_device_id`, `missing_event`, `invalid_batch`, `batch_too_large`, `event_name_too_long`, `event_too_large`, `invalid_event_data`, `missing_message`, `message_too_long`, `invalid_category`, `invalid_feedback` | Malformed request body or a payload ceiling (see Limits). |
| 401 | `missing_api_key`, `invalid_api_key`, or a missing/expired session token | Bad or absent credentials for the header the endpoint expects. |
| 403 | `tracking_disabled` | The game's server-side kill switch is off. Only returned by `POST /api/v1/session`. |
| 429 | `rate_limited` | Per-game ceiling hit: 60 session creations or 600 tracked events per minute. Carries a `Retry-After` header in seconds. |
| 429 | `quota_exceeded` | Monthly event quota reached for this account. Carries a `Retry-After` header, in seconds until the quota resets at the next UTC month. |
| 503 | `storage_unavailable` | Event storage is temporarily unavailable. Carries `Retry-After: 60`; nothing was accepted or charged against quota. |

documents.title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.content:
6. Projects and environments

 

## One title, one project, one game per environment

 

Your development build and your shipped build must not share an event stream, or a week of debugging quietly becomes your retention number. Ravensight keeps them apart by making each one its own game, and groups the games of one title into a project.

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: The three scopes
documents.content:
### The three scopes

 

| Scope | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| Environment, one game | Its own ingest key, its own tracking and history switches, and its own events, sessions, players, funnels, journeys, retention, reports and digests. Labels are fixed: production, staging, development, at most one of each per project. |
| Project, one title | Name and engine, and the environments underneath it. Project-scoped pages read the project rather than one build. |
| Studio, your org | Members and roles, billing and the prepaid balance, the studio context graph, studio notes, cross-game analytics and the audit log. |

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: Picking one
documents.content:
### Picking one

 

The switcher at the top of the sidebar picks a project. Beside it in the header, on the pages whose numbers come from one build, an environment control picks which environment you are looking at. A project with a single environment needs no second choice, and the pages that belong to the whole project do not show the control at all.

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: Managing them
documents.content:
### Managing them

 

**Settings > Projects** is where projects are renamed, merged, and given new environments. Because every existing game was migrated into a project of its own, two environments of the same title can start out as two projects. Ravensight proposes the merge when their names normalize to the same thing and their environment labels do not collide, and nothing is merged until you accept the proposal. Dismiss one and it stays dismissed. You can also move a single environment from one project to another, or delete a project once it is empty.

 

Creating, renaming, merging and deleting all need an admin role or above. Everyone in the studio can read the list.

 

Analytics queries are still keyed on one game, which is why a number on screen always belongs to exactly one environment. A project-level or studio-level number is the same per-game query asked of several games and summed, never a new aggregation with its own rules.

documents.title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.content:
7. Check your integration: the doctor

 

## Check your integration before and after you ship

 

Two layers watch your integration. The dashboard computes implementation health from your game's own live traffic, and a public scanner checks your source tree before you ship. Both feed the same card on your game's Overview page.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: Live implementation health
documents.content:
### Live implementation health

 

Automatic, no setup. The API already sees what your integration does: requests rejected for size, event names exploding in cardinality, payloads brushing the 8KB ceiling, sessions that start but never flush an exit. The Implementation health card on Overview summarizes it over the last 7 days and tells you what to change.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: ravensight doctor
documents.content:
### ravensight doctor

 

A zero-dependency scanner for your project directory. It detects your engine, finds the SDK, and lints the integration statically: event name length and cardinality, oversized inline payloads, missing track calls, and credentials that must never ship inside a game build (an MCP token or a cloud key in your tree is an error; your publishable gt_live ingest key is fine).

 

Run it

 

```
npx ravensight-doctor

# machine readable
npx ravensight-doctor --json

# also submit the report to your dashboard
RAVENSIGHT_INGEST_KEY=gt_live_xxxx \
npx ravensight-doctor --report
```

 

Exit code 0 on pass or warnings, 1 when any error-severity finding exists, so CI can fail the build.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: In CI
documents.content:
### In CI

 

GitHub Actions

 

```
- uses: Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-doctor@v0
  with:
    path: .
    report: true
    api-key: ${'$'}{{ secrets.RAVENSIGHT_INGEST_KEY }}
```

 

A GitLab CI snippet ships in the [ravensight-doctor repo](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-doctor).

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: The report API
documents.content:
### The report API

 

The doctor submits to `POST /api/v1/doctor` with your `X-API-Key` ingest key: an engine, a summary (pass, warn or fail with counts), and up to 100 findings. One report is kept per game, newest wins, and it appears on the Implementation health card alongside the live signals.

documents.section_title: Let your coding agent complete the tracking story
documents.title: Let your coding agent complete the tracking story
documents.content:
8. Check your integration: the instrumentation skill

 

## Let your coding agent complete the tracking story

 

Audit and improve tracking in a new game or one you have already shipped. The Ravensight Instrumentation Skill guides your agent through existing events, missing player journeys, failures, retries, choices and exits.

 

Choose audit-only for recommendations, expand for code changes to an existing integration, or initialize for a new one. Your agent preserves useful events, checks for duplicate or misleading tracking, and produces an event catalog and coverage report with verification evidence.

documents.section_title: Let your coding agent complete the tracking story
documents.title: 1. Choose your agent
documents.content:
### 1. Choose your agent

 

The public [Ravensight Skills repository](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-skills) contains the skill and its references. Choose the installer flag for the agent you use in your game repository.

 

| Agent | Installer flag | How to start |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex | `--agent codex` | `$ravensight-instrumentation` |
| Claude Code | `--agent claude` | `/ravensight-instrumentation` |
| GitHub Copilot | `--agent copilot` | Ask it to use ravensight-instrumentation. |
| Other agents | `--agent generic` | Ask the agent to read the installed SKILL.md and its references. |

documents.section_title: Let your coding agent complete the tracking story
documents.title: 2. Install in your game repository
documents.content:
### 2. Install in your game repository

 

With Node 20 or later, open a terminal in your game directory and run the command below. Replace `codex` with your agent's flag value from the table.

 

```
npx ravensight-skills --agent codex --project .
```

 

This downloads and runs the public installer. It adds skill files, preserves existing content, and leaves game code alone. Add `--dry-run` to preview the destination. Reload your agent's skills or restart its session if it does not discover the new skill.

 

Without Node, copy the complete `skills/ravensight-instrumentation` folder from the repository into your agent's skill directory. Keep `references/` and `agents/` with `SKILL.md`. The [setup guide](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-skills#install) lists the exact directories, update and uninstall steps. To pin an installation to a version, run `npx ravensight-skills@0.1.5 --agent codex --project .` instead.

documents.section_title: Let your coding agent complete the tracking story
documents.title: 3. Choose what the agent should do
documents.content:
### 3. Choose what the agent should do

 

Audit existing tracking without code changes

 

```
Use ravensight-instrumentation to audit our existing tracking.
Report missing, duplicate, or misleading events with source locations.
Do not edit application code.
```

 

Expand tracking in an existing product

 

```
Use ravensight-instrumentation to audit and expand our tracking.
Cover meaningful journeys, decisions, failures, retries and exits.
Preserve useful existing events, implement gaps, validate changes,
and update our event catalog and coverage report.
```

 

Start a new integration

 

```
Use ravensight-instrumentation to integrate Ravensight in this game.
Inspect the engine and SDK, then instrument the player journeys.
```

 

To work on selected code, name the subsystem or files in your request, for example: **Limit edits to inventory and crafting; follow callers and outcomes as needed.** Audit mode reviews existing choices. Expand mode implements missing coverage without duplicating useful events.

documents.section_title: Let your coding agent complete the tracking story
documents.title: 4. Review coverage and verify delivery
documents.content:
### 4. Review coverage and verify delivery

 

The agent produces an event catalog and coverage report, normally in `docs/analytics/events.md` and `docs/analytics/coverage.md`, or updates your existing documents. A chat-only audit can return its findings inline. Review the new events, retained tracking, deferred gaps, volume assumptions, and the checks the agent actually ran.

 

Code inspection, local execution, and events observed arriving are different evidence levels. Use a development environment for runtime verification. Installing the skill alone does not collect events, publish a build, or guarantee complete coverage of every possible player action.

documents.section_title: Let your coding agent complete the tracking story
documents.title: ChatGPT, access and costs
documents.content:
### ChatGPT, access and costs

 

For a client without local skill discovery, provide [SKILL.md](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-skills/blob/main/skills/ravensight-instrumentation/SKILL.md) and its references, then explicitly ask it to follow the workflow. Supply the relevant source or a supported repository connection. Implementation requires editing tools; this pack does not install a connector or grant code access.

 

Local source is sufficient. Optional authorized MCP access can add live evidence and is metered; your agent provider may charge for its own work. Added events can increase event usage. The workflow respects existing collection controls and keeps event volume and payloads bounded.

documents.section_title: Let your coding agent complete the tracking story
documents.title: Updating or troubleshooting
documents.content:
### Updating or troubleshooting

 

If the installer reports different existing content, preserve your local edits before removing the old skill folder and reinstalling. To uninstall, remove that skill folder. If live data is unavailable, the agent can continue locally and must report delivery as unverified. See the repository setup guide for manual loading and supported installation paths.

documents.section_title: Read these docs through MCP
documents.title: Read these docs through MCP
documents.content:
9. Check your integration: Docs MCP

 

## Read these docs through MCP

 

Give your agent searchable Ravensight documentation while it integrates your game or audits existing tracking. Documentation reads are free and require no account, API key, or prepaid balance.

 

This public server reads the documentation on this page. It cannot see your studio, query player data, change your project, or spend Ravensight units. The [analytics MCP](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#mcp) is a separate, authenticated service with its own metering. Your agent provider may still charge for the agent's work.

documents.section_title: Read these docs through MCP
documents.title: 1. Connect your agent
documents.content:
### 1. Connect your agent

 

Use this remote HTTP MCP URL, with authentication set to none:

 

```
https://docs-mcp.ravensight.io/mcp
```

 

Codex CLI

 

```
codex mcp add ravensight-docs --url https://docs-mcp.ravensight.io/mcp
```

 

Claude Code

 

```
claude mcp add --transport http ravensight-docs https://docs-mcp.ravensight.io/mcp
```

 

VS Code / GitHub Copilot: merge into .vscode/mcp.json

 

```
{
  "servers": {
    "ravensight-docs": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://docs-mcp.ravensight.io/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

 

Keep your other server entries when merging configuration. Reload the agent's tools if needed. In another MCP-compatible client, add the same URL as a remote server. In ChatGPT, use a supported custom MCP connection if your account and workspace allow it; connecting the docs does not grant access to your code.

 

Client setup references: [Codex](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp?surface=cli), [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), and [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers). Client interfaces and workspace policies may differ.

documents.section_title: Read these docs through MCP
documents.title: 2. Ask a concrete integration question
documents.content:
### 2. Ask a concrete integration question

 

```
Use ravensight-docs to find the event payload limits and Godot
session setup instructions. Read the relevant sections, cite their
links, and compare them with the SDK version installed in this project.
```

 

| Tool | What it returns |
| --- | --- |
| `search_docs(query, limit?, section?)` | Up to 10 relevant records with excerpts, IDs, source links, and content revisions. An optional section narrows the search. |
| `get_doc(id, offset?, max_chars?, revision?)` | A Markdown record with code examples and tables. For long records, continue at `next_offset` with the same document revision. |

 

Clients that browse MCP resources can open `ravensight-docs://index` and the individual document resources. A section link may point to its parent section when the website has no more specific anchor. The server retrieves documentation; your agent interprets it and should check it against your installed SDK.

documents.section_title: Read these docs through MCP
documents.title: 3. Use it with the instrumentation skill
documents.content:
### 3. Use it with the instrumentation skill

 

The [instrumentation skill](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#instrumentation-skill) supplies the audit and implementation workflow. This server supplies current documentation. They work together, and each remains useful on its own. The skill installer does not add MCP connections or change your agent's settings.

documents.section_title: Read these docs through MCP
documents.title: Freshness, limits, and troubleshooting
documents.content:
### Freshness, limits, and troubleshooting

 

The catalog is generated from this page on every website build. Responses include document and catalog revisions, the last successful source check, and a `stale` flag. Normal refresh is within five minutes. If the source is temporarily unavailable, previously validated content may be served for up to one hour and is marked stale. After that, the server reports unavailable; read this page directly.

 

- **No tools:** confirm the URL ends in `/mcp`, choose remote HTTP, and reload the connection. This service needs no bearer token. Opening the MCP URL in a browser may return 405 because MCP requests use POST.
 
- **Too many requests (429):** pause and retry with backoff. Public capacity is shared; avoid polling or sending the entire codebase as a search query.
 
- **Stale or unavailable:** check [service health](https://docs-mcp.ravensight.io/health) and use the ordinary docs links. A healthy transport alone does not prove telemetry delivery in your game.
 
- **Document changed while paging:** restart at offset 0. Search again for an unknown ID. Narrow broad searches using a section from the index.

 

Send only documentation questions, not credentials, private source, or player data. The server does not call an AI model or store search queries in an application database. Operational request metadata may be recorded by the hosting provider. Source and deployment instructions are in the public [ravensight-docs-mcp repository](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-docs-mcp); the generated [documentation catalog](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/catalog.json) is also available without MCP.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.content:
10. Check your integration: source scan

 

## The gap between what your game does and what it reports

 

Analytics can only answer questions about events you actually send. The source scan reads your code and your live telemetry together, and tells you where the two disagree.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: How it runs
documents.content:
### How it runs

 

Three front doors, one pipeline. Connect GitHub and a push scans itself (below), or send your source as a zip upload up to 100 MB, or as a JSON body of `{ files: [{ path, text }] }` up to 40 MB, which is what makes it easy to post from CI. A cheap model reads the files in batches and writes short notes on what each one does and what it reports. A stronger model then reads those notes alongside a deterministic gather of the last 30 days of your own events, and writes the findings. Neither stage is given tools.

 

Those notes are kept, and your source is not. A scan builds a standing model of the repository: per file, the path, a hash of its text, and our one-line note about it, plus a repository-level read of the architecture, the modules, and which telemetry the code does and does not send. There is nowhere in it to put your code. The next scan compares hashes against that model and re-reads only what changed, which is both why a rescan is priced at a floor rather than by repo size and why the findings get sharper each time: the model that writes them is looking at the whole repository, not at the diff you happened to send. Because it does read the whole repository, a very large one is quoted at its size tier instead of the floor.

 

Your analyst can read that model too, and so can your own agents over MCP, through `get_code_brief`. That is what lets an answer about a funnel that dies at step three come back with the reason: not that players quit, but that nothing in the code reports the step.

 

Only code is read, and only so much of it: eight source extensions, files up to 100 KB, at most 6,000 files, with dependency and build directories skipped. Binaries are detected and dropped rather than counted. Every run carries a hard token budget, so a repo that turns out larger than it looked stops at the budget and reports what it got rather than spending without limit.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: Scanning on every push
documents.content:
### Scanning on every push

 

Connect GitHub once and a push scans what changed, without anybody uploading anything. Open **Code** in the dashboard and press **Connect GitHub**, which installs the Ravensight app on the account or organization that holds your repositories. You choose which repositories it can see, and you can change that on GitHub at any time. Connecting is an owner action, because a connected repository can spend your balance without anybody watching.

 

Ravensight asks for two read permissions and no write permissions: **Contents** and **Metadata**, both read-only. That is enough to read files, the commit tree and a diff between two commits, and it is not enough to push a branch, open a pull request, comment, or change a setting. Nothing in the scanner writes to GitHub.

 

Then attach a repository to a game, on the same screen. One repository belongs to one game: that is what lets a push know whose telemetry to read it against. A game with a client repo and a server repo keeps a separate model of each, and a change to one is never priced as a change to the other.

 

**Only the default branch scans.** A push to a feature branch is acknowledged and ignored, on purpose: the question the scan answers is what your shipped game reports, and a branch is not that yet. If nothing happens after a push, this is the first thing to check.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: What a push spends, and how to stop it
documents.content:
### What a push spends, and how to stop it

 

A push scan charges the balance by itself, up to **$3 a day per repository**. Past that ceiling the scan is queued instead and waits for somebody to approve it in the dashboard, where the price is shown before you agree to it. You can raise the ceiling per repository, or turn auto-charge off entirely with **Scan every push automatically**, in which case every push queues and nothing is ever charged unattended.

 

The ceiling is deliberately lower than the cheapest whole-repository price, and the reason is worth knowing. Usually a push is a diff, and a diff costs $2. Sometimes there is no diff to read: the first push after connecting, a force push, or a rewritten history all leave us nothing to compare against, so the scan reads the whole repository and is priced accordingly. That is exactly the case that must not be charged while nobody is looking, so it goes past the ceiling and waits for you.

 

Disconnecting is on the same screen, per repository or for the whole studio. Pushes stop immediately. Your notes are kept, because you paid for them and they are what keeps the next scan at the rescan price rather than a first-scan price, so reconnecting later does not mean buying the same reading twice. Deleting the game is what deletes them.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: What you get back
documents.content:
### What you get back

 

Findings, not patches. Each one names a kind (`instrumentation_gap` or `risk`), a severity, the file and lines, a short evidence quote, a hypothesis and a suggestion. Nothing rewrites your code, and nothing is committed anywhere.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: What it costs
documents.content:
### What it costs

 

The first scan of a repository is a fixed price by the size of the source that survives the filter, drawn from your prepaid balance: $5 under 250 KB, $10 under 1 MB, $25 under 4 MB and $50 under 16 MB. Past 16 MB of surviving source a scan is refused rather than priced.

 

Every scan after that is priced on what actually changed. We compare a hash of each file you send against the hash in our notes, and only the files that differ are read and paid for: $2 while the changed source is under 250 KB, and otherwise the tier that change set belongs to on its own. Nothing is taken on trust here, and there is no flag you can set to claim a discount. Two consequences follow, both in your favor. Resubmitting a repository with nothing changed in it is free and does not run, because there is no work to do. And a change set is measured against our notes rather than against the last submission's size, so a 900 KB edit to a 1 MB repository is priced as 900 KB of work instead of as a second full scan.

 

Pricing is per repository, not per game. A game with a client repo and a server repo keeps a separate model of each, and a change to one is never priced as a change to the other.

 

Sizing is free: ask for a quote first and you see the price, what changed, and the token estimate before any money moves. Scanning needs an admin role or above, because it spends the balance. Connecting a code host so that pushes can scan on their own is a step further and is owner only: a scan spends a quoted amount once, while a connected repository is standing permission to spend. Whether that connection is available at all depends on how the deployment you are using is configured, so treat a visible connect button as an offer rather than a promise.

 

If a run stops early on its token budget you pay for the source it actually read, at that size's tier and never more than you were quoted, and you keep the findings and notes it produced. If a run fails outright you are refunded in full and its notes are unwound, so the next scan is priced honestly as a first scan rather than as a cheap diff against a half-written model.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: What each page is for
documents.content:
11. Reading your data: the dashboard

 

## What each page is for

 

The sidebar is grouped by what you are doing rather than by which database the answer comes from. The order below is the order the sidebar puts them in.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Build
documents.content:
### Build

 

Project-scoped: these read the title, not one of its builds.

 

- **Brainstorm.** A board of cards beside a partner that has read your studio's own findings, patterns, touchpoints and sales. See [Brainstorm](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#brainstorm).
 
- **Design.** Your design documents, and a chat that has read your studio's findings before it proposes an edit. See [Design studio](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#design-studio).
 
- **Code scan.** What your code reports against what your telemetry actually receives. See [Source scan](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#code-scan).
 
- **Playtest.** Jobs, briefs, findings and reports from AI personas playing your build. See [Playtest](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#playtest).

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Live data
documents.content:
### Live data

 

Environment-scoped: every number here comes from the events one build sent. Overview, Player insights and Events each carry a **Real players** select, because persona sessions are real rows in the same store and are excluded by default.

 

- **Overview.** Daily active players, top events, lifetime totals, retention, the level funnel and the implementation health card. Results are cached per scope and range, so a repeat visit does not re-run the warehouse queries; a missing or expired snapshot still fetches fresh.
 
- **Player insights.** A triage board of the sessions the backend flagged, with the plain-language signals behind each call. See [how the detections read your events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#detection-rules).
 
- **Events.** Raw events newest first, filterable by name and paged, with expandable payload rows.
 
- **Funnels.** An ordered sequence of two to eight event names: who reached each step, how many were lost against the step before, and the average and median gap into each one. Count players or sessions, and filter by an event property.
 
- **Journeys.** The level-to-level graph, where players stop, churn-heavy transitions, loops and estimated common paths. Only on deployments with journey graphs configured.
 
- **Player Reports.** The inbox for what players sent from inside the game. See [Player Reports](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#player-reports). A game without the report overlay sees its free-form feedback here instead, summarized by sentiment and theme and searchable by meaning.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Understand
documents.content:
### Understand

 

- **Studio Intelligence.** An investigation that ties a question to its evidence to a decision. See [Studio Intelligence](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#studio-intelligence).
 
- **Huginn (AI analyst).** Ask in plain English; Huginn picks its own read-only tools and answers with the numbers it used. Conversations are listable, resumable, renameable and deletable. See [Huginn, the AI analyst](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#analyst).
 
- **Muninn (studio memory).** Everything your studio has learned, across every game. See [Muninn, studio memory](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#studio-context).

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Studio
documents.content:
### Studio

 

- **Marketing.** What you did outside the game and the lift the platform measured afterwards. See [Marketing memory](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#marketing-memory).
 
- **Sales.** Its own page directly below Marketing in the Studio navigation. Record what each title earned, filter the ledger, compare totals by currency, explore a 90 day launch curve, and import store exports. See the [Sales ledger](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#sales-ledger).
 
- **Audit log.** Who did what in the org. Owner and admin only.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: In the footer
documents.content:
### In the footer

 

Settings sits below the groups rather than inside them, because it is global to the account rather than to the selected game. Its tabs are Usage and billing and Payment history (both owner only), Projects, Team, Huginn, MCP access, Playtest CLI and Appearance. The events meter beside it shows this month against the free allowance.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: How the built-in detections read your events
documents.content:
### How the built-in detections read your events

 

The level funnel, journeys, and the player flags are computed from your event names and the place fields, with no configuration. Name your events accordingly and they light up.

 

- **Deaths** are events whose name contains `died`, `destroyed`, or `killed` (lowercase substring match, so `player_died` and `ship_destroyed` both count).
 
- **Level starts** are names containing `start`, `begin`, or `enter`; **completions** contain `complet`, `finish`, `win`, or `clear`.
 
- **An explicit `rs_kind` comes first.** Set `rs_kind` in the event data to `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death`, or `none` and the level funnel, per-level deaths, journeys and the death count read it before the name. `none` opts an event out, so `checkout_started` with `rs_kind: "none"` is not a level start. An unknown value falls through to the name match. Keys that start with `rs_` are reserved for Ravensight. The rage quit rule below still reads names only.
 
- **`level`, `location` and `track` fold into one place.** The first non-empty one wins, in that order. The funnel, per-level deaths, and journeys only see events that have a place. It is any string that names a place or mode in your game: a level id, an encounter, a scene name.
 
- **Rage quit likely** flags a session with 3 or more deaths in its last 5 events, 3 or more deaths at the same level (counting `died`/`destroyed` names), or a final event containing `died` followed by more than 10 minutes of silence inside the queried window.
 
- **Potentially stuck** flags a session that repeats one event 10 or more times at the same level while the whole session has fewer than 20 events. The same event at a new level each time is movement, not stuck.
 
- **Highly engaged** flags a session with at least 20 events at more than 2 events per minute and fewer than 5 deaths.

 

Every flag comes back with the plain-language indicators that triggered it, so you can always see why a session was tagged.

documents.section_title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.content:
12. Ask your events a question in plain English

 

## Huginn, the AI analyst

 

Huginn, the AI analyst, lives under **Understand > Huginn**. It picks its own read-only tools, runs them against the game you have selected, and answers with the numbers it used. A completed question is one shared AI unit, including every tool call it made on the way.

documents.section_title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.title: The tools it reaches for
documents.content:
### The tools it reaches for

 

`get_overview`, `query_players`, `query_levels`, `get_retention`, `get_history`, `get_metrics`, `get_funnel`, `get_property_breakdown` and `search_feedback` cover the numbers and what players wrote. `get_code_brief` reads the source scan's notes, `list_playtest_jobs`, `list_playtest_findings` and `get_playtest_report` read playtests, and `list_touchpoints` and `get_sales` read marketing memory and the sales ledger. On deployments with journey graphs, `get_journeys`, `find_bottlenecks` and `get_top_paths` read those. When nothing else answers, it writes SQL with [run_sql](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#run-sql). Every tool is read-only, and the game it reads is the one you selected, never an argument the model can change.

documents.section_title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.title: Analyst context you write yourself
documents.content:
### Analyst context you write yourself

 

Findings are extracted by a model. Analyst context is the opposite: it is what you write, and the analyst is told to trust it over its own reading of the data. There are two levels, both inserted into the prompt verbatim and ahead of the findings. Game context lives in **Settings > Huginn** and holds up to 2,000 characters of facts about one game. Studio notes hold up to 1,000 characters of facts that are true across every game in the studio. A note like "levels 5 through 7 are an intentional difficulty spike" or "we ship weekly builds on Fridays" heads off a wrong conclusion before the analyst reaches for a tool. Writing either needs a member role or above; reading them needs nothing extra.

documents.section_title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.title: The same question across every game
documents.content:
### The same question across every game

 

Three questions can be asked of the whole studio rather than one game: the headline metrics, a funnel, and an event property's breakdown. The analyst has them as `compare_metrics`, `compare_funnel` and `compare_property`, and the API exposes them under `/api/v1/studio/analytics/...`. This is how a problem in one game is told apart from a habit of the studio: if the tutorial loses the same share of players in all three of your games, the tutorial design is the finding. Studio totals are sums and conversions are weighted by volume. There is deliberately no studio median, because the median of medians is not the median.

 

A studio answer covers at most 12 games. When more were eligible the response says so rather than presenting twelve games as the studio: `studio.truncated` is true and `studio.omittedGames` counts the games left out. A property breakdown also carries `studio.other`, the count of events whose value is not in the merged top list.

documents.section_title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.content:
13. AI analyst: run_sql and the events schema

 

## Your events, queryable directly

 

`run_sql` is available both as an MCP tool and to the in-dashboard analyst. It is a real SELECT against your event store, not a canned report.

documents.section_title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.title: events table columns
documents.content:
### events table columns

 

| Column | Type |
| --- | --- |
| `game_id` | String |
| `device_id` | String |
| `session_id` | String |
| `event_name` | String |
| `ts` | DateTime64(3, 'UTC') |
| `level` | String |
| `platform` | String |
| `game_version` | String |
| `payload` | String, arbitrary JSON |
| `props` | Map(String, String) of the payload's top-level keys, so `props['difficulty']` reads a property directly. Values are text: cast before comparing numerically. |

documents.section_title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.title: Rules
documents.content:
### Rules

 

- **SELECT only.** A single `SELECT` or `WITH ... SELECT` statement. Writes, DDL, and settings changes are rejected before the query runs.
 
- **No comments, extra statements, dollar signs or table functions.** `--`, `/* */`, `#`, and semicolons (beyond one optional trailing one) are all rejected, as is a `$` anywhere in the query and any table-function call such as `FROM name(...)`.
 
- **events only.** The only readable table is `ravensight.events`, plus any CTEs you define in the same query. Other table names, table functions, and cross-database reads are rejected.
 
- **The game filter is automatic.** Every reference to `events` is rewritten to a subquery scoped to your own `game_id` before it runs. Do not write your own `game_id` predicate: you cannot see or query another game's rows regardless.
 
- **Row cap.** Results are capped at 100 rows when usage metering against the prepaid balance is on, and at 200 rows where metering is off, no matter what `LIMIT` you write. The same cap applies to the analyst and to MCP.
 
- **Query and time limits.** Queries are capped at 4,000 characters and run with `readonly=1` at the database level. A metered query gets 3 seconds of execution and reads at most 1,000,000 rows and 64 MB; with metering off the limit is 15 seconds.

documents.section_title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.title: Example
documents.content:
### Example

 

Deaths by level, most first:

 

```
select level, count() as deaths
from events
where event_name = 'player_death'
group by level
order by deaths desc
```

documents.section_title: Your analytics as tools for your own agents
documents.title: Your analytics as tools for your own agents
documents.content:
14. Analytics MCP

 

## Your analytics as tools for your own agents

 

Ravensight runs an MCP server at `/mcp` so you can ask Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or anything else that speaks MCP about your game's data directly, without opening the dashboard.

documents.section_title: Your analytics as tools for your own agents
documents.title: Connect it
documents.content:
### Connect it

 

Mint a personal access token from the dashboard's **Settings > MCP access** tab. It looks like `gt_mcp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx` and is sent as a Bearer token.

 

```
claude mcp add --transport http ravensight https://api.ravensight.io/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer gt_mcp_..."
```

 

The endpoint is a stateless streamable HTTP transport: every request is handled independently, with no session to resume and nothing to clean up between calls.

documents.section_title: Your analytics as tools for your own agents
documents.title: Tools
documents.content:
### Tools

 

The game analytics tools are Huginn's own toolset, the same read-only tools the AI analyst reaches for in the dashboard. Every tool below that takes a `game_id` checks it against the games your token's owner actually has, on every single call rather than once when the token was minted: a token can never read another tenant's game, and a teammate removed from your studio loses access on their next call.

 

A token is bound to the studio that was selected when it was minted. Every `game_id` is checked against that studio and, when the token is limited to some projects, against those projects, whatever the billing mode. If you were invited to another studio, switch to it in the dashboard before minting a token for it; a token minted in your own studio cannot read the other studio's games.

 

MCP calls are metered usage on the same event meter as everything else: one call weighs 100,000 events, which is $0.05 once the included million is spent, and a write costs exactly what a read costs. MCP needs an account that has loaded a prepaid balance at least once. Each token also carries its own monthly cap in **Settings > MCP access**, and a token that has spent its cap is refused rather than charged further, so a looping agent cannot empty the account on one credential. A call that fails is not charged. Your external AI client may charge separately for its own model usage.

 

**A token reads by default.** The write tools below need a token an owner has switched **Allow writes** on for, on the token's own form in **Settings > MCP access**. Nothing about money, tokens, team members, games or projects is writable over MCP at all: a write-capable token can record marketing touchpoints, keep the sales ledger, store reference documents and put cards on a brainstorm board, and that is the whole list. Every write is written to your audit log with the tool name and how many rows it created, updated or rejected, never the rows themselves.

 

The studio-wide comparisons are not MCP tools. Asking the same metric, funnel or property of every game at once is something Huginn does in the dashboard, and the API exposes under `/api/v1/studio/analytics/...`; an MCP client asks `list_games` and then one game at a time.

 

Some of them are written to your org's audit log: `run_sql`, every studio-context read, and every write. Those are the calls that can pull the most out of an account, or put the most into it, in one request, so if a token ever goes astray you can see exactly what was taken and what was added. The log records the tool name and the game, never your query text and never what a write said.

 

#### list_games

 

List your games: gameId, name, and whether tracking is enabled. Every other tool needs a gameId from this list. One entry per environment, so a title with a production and a development build appears twice; the project grouping is dashboard-side and is not returned here.

 

#### get_overview(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Headline analytics for one game: daily active players, totals, median session length, top events.

 

#### query_players(game_id, from?, to?, limit?, skip?)

 

Per-session behavior rows with rage-quit, stuck, and engaged flags and the indicators behind them.

 

#### query_levels(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Per-level funnel: starts, completions, deaths, completion rate.

 

#### get_retention(game_id, from?, to?)

 

D1/D7 retention, overall and by first-seen cohort.

 

#### get_metrics(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Players, sessions, new versus returning, and session length as both an average and a median. New means first seen ever, not first seen in the window you asked about.

 

#### get_funnel(game_id, steps, windowSeconds?, countBy?, filters?, from?, to?)

 

An ordered conversion funnel over 2 to 8 event names: how many reached each step, the share lost from the step before, and the gap into each step as an average and a median. Steps must happen in order inside the conversion window, so doing step two first does not count as converting. Count players or sessions, and filter by event property.

 

#### get_property_breakdown(game_id, property, limit?, from?, to?)

 

How one event property's values are distributed: ranked values with event and player counts, plus a daily series. Reads the top-level keys of the payload your game sends, so ask for the key name. An unknown key returns an empty breakdown, which is an answer.

 

#### get_usage_rate()

 

What a metered MCP call costs, the result and byte ceilings a tool answer is held to, and the header to send when you retry one. Free: ask it first if your agent wants to know the price before it spends.

 

#### get_history(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Lifetime totals and long-range trends from stored rollups, beyond the 90-day raw window: lifetime players, sessions and events, a daily active player series, summable totals and merged top events for the window you ask for. This is the tool for month over month, year over year, and all-time questions.

 

#### search_studio_context(query, game_id?, limit?)
